newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Any ACPC coffee deal seen as impossible to enforce.
newsitem.headline: Any ACPC coffee deal seen as impossible to enforce.

text.p: A proposal by African producers to trim coffee exports could win approval at the special meeting of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) now being held in Brazil, but it may also be impossible to enforce the deal, Southeast Asian traders said on Tuesday.

African coffee producers want ACPC members to slice exports in the first half of 1997 by 2.5 million 60-kg bags to shore up prices. The 14-member group will consider the proposal in Rio de Janeiro on Friday.

Indonesia, the world's third biggest coffee producer, has expressed reservations about the proposal and demanded the Africans should convince Vietnam, which is not a member of the organisation and its regional competitor, to join the ACPC.
"They might come up with an agreement. But it's going to be a bucket with a lot of holes in it," a senior dealer for a European trading house told Reuters.

"It's unworkable," declared a veteran trader for another European-based coffee house. "How will you control thousands and thousands of private exporters unless they sell their crop to the government."
Traders said the Brazilian government's estimate for its 1997/98 coffee crop will boost prices over the next few months and render a retention scheme unnecessary.
"There's going to be a huge shortfall in coffee. Prices will go up without anybody controlling the market. There's really no need for a reduction plan," one trader said

The head of the primary commodities department of Brazil's Industry and Commerce Ministry forecast on Monday that the country's 1997/98 coffee crop would reach only 18-20 million 60-kg bags, versus 25 million in 1996/97.
Brazil is the world's largest producer of coffee.
News that Vietnam is considering membership in the ACPC but is not ready to join the group meant Indonesia will have to shoulder the bulk of any cut in exports, the dealers said.

"It's tough. The people who will have to cut their exports are the Indonesians. Countries like the Ivory Coast and Uganda have been aggressive sellers of their crop. The only country coming up with a big crop is Indonesia," one dealer said.
"The Indonesians are pretty wary about the whole thing because they may get screwed by Vietnam," another dealer for a Singapore-based commodity house said.

Members of the InterAfrican Coffee Organisation (IACO) gave assurances at a recent Asia Coffee conference in Ho Chi Minh city in Vietnam that any reduction plan, to be presented at the ACPC meeting in Brazil, will be fair.
